blocks.body:
Is $n=2^{89}-1$ prime? Trial division would test divisors up to $\sqrt n\approx2.49\times10^{13}$, which is slow but feasible on a computer. For a $300$-digit number, the size RSA key generation needs routinely, trial division would need about $10^{150}$ steps, far beyond any computer. Yet such numbers are tested in a fraction of a second.

The trick is to test a consequence of primality that is cheap to compute, without trying to find a factor. Fermat's little theorem supplies one; it has a famous blind spot, the Carmichael numbers such as $561$, and repairing it leads to the Miller–Rabin test used in practice. A different idea gave the first unconditional deterministic polynomial-time test, by Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena in 2002.

blocks.title: Fast modular exponentiation
blocks.body:
All the tests below need $a^k\bmod n$ for huge $k$. Computing $a^k$ first is hopeless, but reducing modulo $n$ after every multiplication keeps numbers below $n^2$, and repeated squaring needs only about $2\log_2k$ multiplications. Write $k$ in binary; compute $a,a^2,a^4,a^8,\dots$ by squaring; multiply together the powers corresponding to the binary digits $1$. For example $a^{13}=a^8\cdot a^4\cdot a$. For a $2048$-bit modulus this is a few thousand multiplications of $2048$-bit numbers, which a laptop does in milliseconds.

"Polynomial time" for a number $n$ means time bounded by a power of the number of digits, i.e. by $(\log n)^C$. Trial division takes about $\sqrt n=e^{\frac12\log n}$ steps, which is exponential in the number of digits.

blocks.title: The Fermat test
blocks.body:
Let $n\ge2$ and let $a$ be an integer not divisible by $n$. If

$$a^{n-1}\not\equiv1\pmod n,$$

then $n$ is composite.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: If $n$ were prime, then $n\nmid a$ would give $a^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n$ by [[fermat-euler|Fermat's little theorem]]. This is the contrapositive.

blocks.title: Witnesses, liars and pseudoprimes
blocks.body:
The hypothesis $n\nmid a$ is needed: for $n=5$ and $a=5$ we have $a^{n-1}\equiv0\not\equiv1$, yet $5$ is prime. In practice one takes $1< a< n-1$.

If $a^{n-1}\not\equiv1$, the base $a$ is called a Fermat witness for $n$; the test proves compositeness without producing a factor. If $a^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n$ but $n$ is composite, $a$ is a Fermat liar and $n$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to base $a$. The smallest pseudoprime to base $2$ is $341=11\cdot31$: since $2^{10}=1024=3\cdot341+1$, we get $2^{340}=(2^{10})^{34}\equiv1\pmod{341}$. Base $3$ exposes it: $3^{340}\equiv56\pmod{341}$.

One might hope that every composite $n$ has many witnesses. For most composites that is true: the liars coprime to $n$ form a subgroup of the group of units modulo $n$, so if there is one witness coprime to $n$, at least half of the units are witnesses. The trouble is that some composites have no coprime witnesses at all.

blocks.title: Carmichael number
blocks.body:
A Carmichael number is a composite $n$ such that $a^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n$ for every integer $a$ coprime to $n$.

For such $n$ the Fermat test can only succeed by stumbling on a base that shares a factor with $n$, which is as hard as finding a factor by trial division.

blocks.title: Korselt's criterion
blocks.body: A composite number $n$ is a Carmichael number if and only if $n$ is squarefree and $p-1\mid n-1$ for every prime $p\mid n$.

blocks.title: Proof of the sufficiency
blocks.body:
We prove the direction used to recognise Carmichael numbers. Suppose $n=p_1p_2\cdots p_k$ with distinct primes and $p_i-1\mid n-1$ for each $i$. Let $\gcd(a,n)=1$. For each $i$, $p_i\nmid a$, so $a^{p_i-1}\equiv1\pmod{p_i}$, and raising to the power $(n-1)/(p_i-1)$ gives $a^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod{p_i}$. The $p_i$ are distinct primes, so their product $n$ divides $a^{n-1}-1$.

The converse uses primitive roots (see [[order-primroot]]): if $p\mid n$, take $a$ that is a primitive root modulo $p$ (modulo $p^2$ if $p^2\mid n$) and $\equiv1$ modulo the part of $n$ coprime to $p$ (possible by the Chinese remainder theorem); then $a^{n-1}\equiv1$ forces $p-1\mid n-1$, and in the case $p^2\mid n$ it would force $p(p-1)\mid n-1$, impossible because $p\mid n$. We omit the details.

blocks.title: Carmichael numbers and square roots of one
blocks.body:
Carmichael numbers exist: $561=3\cdot11\cdot17$ is squarefree and $2$, $10$, $16$ all divide $560$, so by Korselt's criterion it is a Carmichael number, and it is the smallest. The next ones are $1105=5\cdot13\cdot17$ and $1729=7\cdot13\cdot19$. Alford, Granville and Pomerance proved in 1994 that there are infinitely many. So the Fermat test alone can never be a reliable primality test.

The repair uses one more property of primes. Modulo a prime $p$, the congruence $x^2\equiv1$ means $p\mid(x-1)(x+1)$, so $x\equiv\pm1$. Modulo a composite odd $n$ with two different prime factors there are other square roots of $1$; for instance $67^2=4489=8\cdot561+1$, so $67^2\equiv1\pmod{561}$ while $67\not\equiv\pm1$. Finding such a root proves $n$ composite, and even factors it, since $n\mid(x-1)(x+1)$ without dividing either factor.

blocks.title: Strong probable prime property
blocks.body:
Let $n$ be an odd prime and write $n-1=2^sd$ with $d$ odd. Then for every $a$ with $n\nmid a$, either

$$a^d\equiv1\pmod n\qquad\text{or}\qquad a^{2^rd}\equiv-1\pmod n\ \text{ for some } 0\le r< s.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: Consider the sequence $a^d,a^{2d},a^{4d},\dots,a^{2^sd}$, each term the square of the previous one. The last term is $a^{n-1}\equiv1$ by Fermat. If the first term is $1$ we are done. Otherwise there is a first term equal to $1$, say $a^{2^{r+1}d}$ with $0\le r< s$, and the term before it, $x=a^{2^rd}$, satisfies $x^2\equiv1$ and $x\not\equiv1$. Since $n$ is prime, $x\equiv-1$.

blocks.title: The Miller–Rabin test
blocks.body:
The Miller–Rabin test on an odd $n>3$: write $n-1=2^sd$, choose a base $a$ with $1< a< n-1$, compute $a^d$ and then square up to $s-1$ times. If the sequence starts with $1$ or contains $-1$ before the end, $n$ passes for base $a$ (it is a strong probable prime to base $a$). Otherwise $n$ is certainly composite and $a$ is a strong witness.

The test is strong because liars are rare. Rabin and Monier showed independently (both published in 1980) that for odd composite $n>9$ at most $\varphi(n)/4$ of the bases $1\le a< n$ are strong liars. We omit the proof. Consequently, with $k$ independent random bases, a composite number passes all rounds with probability at most $4^{-k}$; forty rounds give an error bound below $10^{-24}$, and for random inputs (as opposed to adversarially chosen ones) the true error is far smaller.

Two refinements are worth knowing. Assuming the [[grh|generalized Riemann hypothesis]], every odd composite $n$ has a strong witness $a<2(\log n)^2$ (Bach, 1990, sharpening Miller's 1976 argument), which would make the test deterministic and polynomial-time. And small inputs can be handled by fixed bases: the smallest strong pseudoprime to base $2$ is $2047=23\cdot89$, and the smallest to both bases $2$ and $3$ is $1373653$, so bases $2$ and $3$ alone decide primality of every $n<1373653$.

blocks.title: The Solovay–Strassen test
blocks.body: [[quadratic-residues|Euler's criterion]] gives another test. For an odd prime $n$ and $n\nmid a$, $a^{(n-1)/2}\equiv\left(\frac an\right)\pmod n$. For odd composite $n$ the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac an\right)$ can still be computed quickly by quadratic reciprocity, without factoring, so one can test whether $a^{(n-1)/2}\equiv\left(\frac an\right)\pmod n$. Solovay and Strassen (1977) showed that for odd composite $n$ at most half of the units are liars for this test, because, unlike the Fermat liars, the Euler liars can never be all the units. Miller–Rabin is at least as strong for each base and is the one used in practice.

blocks.title: The polynomial identity behind AKS
blocks.body:
Let $n\ge2$ and $\gcd(a,n)=1$. Then $n$ is prime if and only if

$$(X+a)^n\equiv X^n+a\pmod n$$

as polynomials in $\mathbb Z[X]$, i.e. coefficient by coefficient.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
The coefficient of $X^k$ in $(X+a)^n-(X^n+a)$ is $\binom nk a^{n-k}$ for $0< k< n$, and the constant term is $a^n-a$.

If $n$ is prime, $n\mid\binom nk$ for $0< k< n$ (the numerator $n!$ contains the prime $n$ and the denominator $k!(n-k)!$ does not), and $a^n\equiv a$ by Fermat. So the identity holds.

If $n$ is composite, let $q$ be a prime factor and $q^m$ the exact power of $q$ dividing $n$. In $\binom nq=\dfrac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-q+1)}{q!}$ the numerator contains exactly $m$ factors of $q$ (only the term $n$ is divisible by $q$), and $q!$ contains exactly one. So $q^m\nmid\binom nq$. Since $\gcd(a,q)=1$, the coefficient $\binom nq a^{n-q}$ of $X^q$ is not divisible by $q^m$, hence not by $n$, and the identity fails.

blocks.title: Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena
blocks.body:
Checking the identity directly needs $n$ coefficients, which is too many. Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena's idea (2002; published in the Annals of Mathematics in 2004) is to check it only modulo $X^r-1$ and $n$, for a suitable small $r$ (polynomial in $\log n$) and for a range of values of $a$ up to roughly $\sqrt r\log n$. Their main theorem says this smaller set of checks still characterises primes, once small factors and perfect powers are excluded. The result was the first unconditional deterministic polynomial-time primality test; the original running time was about $(\log n)^{12}$, later improved to about $(\log n)^6$ by Lenstra and Pomerance.

In practice AKS is much slower than the alternatives. Software generates primes with Miller–Rabin (often combined with a Lucas test, as in the Baillie–PSW test, for which no composite that passes is known), and when a certificate is wanted, uses elliptic curve primality proving.
Show that $341$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to base $2$, and that the strong test with base $2$ detects that it is composite.
blocks.solution:
We saw $2^{10}\equiv1\pmod{341}$, so $2^{340}\equiv1$: base $2$ is a Fermat liar.

For the strong test, $340=2^2\cdot85$, so $s=2$, $d=85$. Since $2^{10}\equiv1$, $2^{85}=2^{80}\cdot2^5\equiv32$, and $2^{170}\equiv32^2=1024\equiv1\pmod{341}$. The sequence is $32,1,1$: it does not start with $1$ and never reaches $-1\equiv340$. So $32$ is a square root of $1$ other than $\pm1$, and $341$ is composite. Indeed $\gcd(32-1,341)=31$ and $\gcd(32+1,341)=11$ recover the factors.

blocks.body: Verify that $561$ is a Carmichael number, then run the strong test on it with base $2$.
blocks.solution:
$561=3\cdot11\cdot17$ is squarefree and $560=2\cdot280=10\cdot56=16\cdot35$, so Korselt's criterion applies.

Now $560=2^4\cdot35$, so $s=4$, $d=35$. Repeated squaring modulo $561$ gives

$$2^{35}\equiv263,\quad2^{70}\equiv166,\quad2^{140}\equiv67,\quad2^{280}\equiv1,\quad2^{560}\equiv1.$$

The sequence does not start with $1$, and the term before the first $1$ is $67\not\equiv-1$. So base $2$ is a strong witness and $561$ is composite, even though no base coprime to $561$ is a Fermat witness. As a bonus, $\gcd(66,561)=33$ and $\gcd(68,561)=17$.

blocks.title: Carmichael numbers have at least three prime factors
blocks.body: Prove that every Carmichael number is odd and has at least three prime factors.
blocks.solution:
Odd: if $n>2$ is even, take $a=n-1$, which is coprime to $n$. Then $a^{n-1}\equiv(-1)^{n-1}=-1\pmod n$ because $n-1$ is odd, and $-1\not\equiv1$ since $n>2$. So no even $n>2$ is Carmichael (and $2$ is prime).

At least three factors: by Korselt, a Carmichael number is squarefree, and it is composite, so it has at least two prime factors. Suppose $n=pq$ with primes $p< q$. Korselt gives $q-1\mid n-1$. But

$$n-1=pq-1=p(q-1)+(p-1),$$

so $q-1\mid p-1$. This is impossible because $0< p-1< q-1$. Hence $n$ has at least three prime factors.

blocks.body:
- The Fermat test needs $n\nmid a$; with $a$ a multiple of $n$ it would "prove" primes composite.
- Passing a probabilistic test is evidence, not proof. "Probable prime" is the correct name for a number that passed.
- The $4^{-k}$ bound needs bases chosen at random independently of $n$. A fixed list of bases can be defeated by composites constructed for that list.
- Miller–Rabin is deterministic only for $n$ below explicit bounds or assuming GRH; without either, it remains probabilistic.
- Primality testing and factoring are different problems. Tests decide primality in polynomial time, while no polynomial-time factoring algorithm is known on classical computers; RSA depends on exactly this gap.

Large primes are the raw material of [[rsa]]: a $2048$-bit modulus needs two random $1024$-bit primes, and by the [[pnt|prime number theorem]] a random odd number of that size is prime with probability about $2/\ln(2^{1024})\approx1/355$, so a few hundred candidates suffice. The tests rest on [[fermat-euler]], [[quadratic-residues]] and the structure of units modulo $n$ from [[order-primroot]]. The conditional deterministic version of Miller–Rabin is one of the algorithmic consequences of the [[grh]]. Diffie–Hellman also needs large primes, often of the form $p=2q+1$ with $q$ prime, see [[discrete-log]]. Elliptic curve primality proving uses the group structure of [[elliptic-curves]] over [[finite-fields]].

1. Use the binary expansion of $340$ to compute $3^{340}\bmod341$ by repeated squaring, and check that you get $56$.
2. Show that $1105$ and $1729$ are Carmichael numbers using Korselt's criterion.
3. Prove that if $n$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to base $2$, then so is $2^n-1$. (Hint: if $n\mid2^n-2$, then $2^n-1\mid2^{2^n-2}-1$.)
4. Find all strong liars for $n=25$, and compare their number with $\varphi(25)/4$.
